Confluent just introduced **Streamhouse** — an open data architecture designed specifically for AI workloads.

This is a meaningful architectural shift worth paying attention to. As AI applications demand real-time, reliable data pipelines, the gap between traditional data lakehouses and streaming infrastructure is becoming a genuine bottleneck. Streamhouse positions itself as the answer: combining the openness of a lakehouse with the low-latency guarantees of stream processing.

For data engineers, this signals a few things:
→ AI-ready data architecture is no longer optional — it's the new baseline
→ The boundary between batch and streaming is continuing to collapse
→ Open architectures are gaining ground against proprietary lock-in

Confluent has long championed Apache Kafka as the backbone of real-time data. Framing their platform around an "open data architecture for AI" suggests they're doubling down on stream processing as the foundation for modern AI pipelines — not just ETL.

If you're designing data infrastructure today, the question isn't whether to support real-time data — it's whether your architecture can scale it for AI.

Worth keeping an eye on how this competes with Databricks' Lakehouse and emerging players in the space.

Postgres isn't slow — your storage is.

A new deep-dive from ClickHouse engineers breaks down a common misconception: teams often blame PostgreSQL's query engine for performance issues when the real bottleneck is storage I/O.

Key takeaways:
• Disk latency and throughput constraints account for the majority of "slow Postgres" complaints
• Proper storage configuration (NVMe vs. spinning disk, RAID setups, filesystem tuning) can yield dramatic query speedups without touching a single index
• Cloud-managed Postgres instances are especially susceptible — default storage tiers are rarely optimized for heavy analytical workloads

This matters for Data Engineers because storage architecture decisions are often made at infrastructure setup and rarely revisited — even as data volumes grow 10x.

Before optimizing your queries, vacuum settings, or connection pooling, audit your storage layer. It's frequently the lowest-hanging fruit with the highest ROI.

The lesson generalizes beyond Postgres: in data-intensive systems, compute gets the glory but storage wins the race.
